foundations.title: How an LLM works
foundations.question: When an AI gives a confident answer, does it actually understand what it is saying?
foundations.concept: A large language model predicts the next likely piece of text from patterns it learned and from the context it is given. It does not look facts up unless a system connects it to a data source.
foundations.risk: Fluent text can still be wrong, manipulated, or built on untrusted context.

foundations.title: From model to agent
foundations.question: What makes an AI agent different from a chatbot?
foundations.concept: An agent combines a model with instructions, tools and data. The model proposes an action; application code and security controls decide what may actually run.
foundations.risk: Tools raise the stakes. A bad proposal matters more when it can trigger a real action.

foundations.title: Tools and MCP
foundations.question: Who decides whether an agent may use a tool?
foundations.concept: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a standard way for an agent to call tools. A tool call is a request. A separate authorization control compares it with what the agent was granted.
foundations.risk: A request is not authorization, and an authorization decision is not proof the tool ran.

foundations.title: Telemetry and evidence
foundations.question: How do you prove what an agent actually did?
foundations.concept: Systems record events as they work: a control decision, a tool starting, a pipeline stopping. Investigators answer questions from those events, citing which event supports each claim.
foundations.risk: Never infer execution from a decision, or safety from missing events.

loandesk.question: Which control decided whether the review note could be filed?
loandesk.answer: CTRL-LOANDESK-001, the policy engine inside AcmeBank.

loandesk.question: In the BASELINE attack policy said ALLOW. What does that tell you?
loandesk.answer: The tool, scope and applicant were valid; the note content was never checked.

loandesk.question: What did the HARDENED posture change?
loandesk.answer: The note must be exactly one reason code, otherwise the call is denied before its handler runs.

loandesk.question: Which recorded event proves that a handler actually began?

mcp.question: Why is `lookup_customer_tier` DENY instead of ERROR in the defended profile?
mcp.answer: The tool is registered (known) but not granted to `acme-agent-mcp-001`. Known-ungranted is an authorization failure → DENY (`tool_not_granted`). ERROR is reserved for unknown tools, malformed arguments, and control-evaluation failures.

mcp.question: Why is an unknown tool ERROR?
mcp.answer: Unknown means the name is not in the registry. CTRL-MCP-001 cannot grant what it does not know. Decision is ERROR `unknown_tool`, handler count 0, no `mcp.started`. Do not call that DENY.

mcp.question: Does ALLOW prove the tool executed?
mcp.answer: No. ALLOW is the control decision. On BASELINE, Q-MCP-AUTHZ shows `executed=false` on the ALLOW row. Execution begins at `mcp.started`.

mcp.question: What proves the handler actually began?
mcp.answer: Runtime: `handler_invoke_count` / registry spy. Telemetry corroboration: `event.name=agentsec.mcp.started` with `operation.executed=true`. ALLOW alone is not enough.

mcp.question: Why is `mcp.failed` not prevention?
mcp.answer: `mcp.failed` means the handler began and then errored (`executed=true`, `outcome=error`). Prevention is DENY/ERROR before start (`executed=false`, `outcome=prevented`, handler count 0).

mcp.question: Why can't zero Splunk events alone prove the handler never executed?
mcp.answer: Export can be incomplete. Absence in a partial copy looks like DENY. You need runtime handler count plus complete local `events.jsonl`, then Splunk as corroboration of that copy.

mcp.question: Why are MCP tool results classified as `untrusted_data`?
mcp.answer: INV-002: retrieved or returned content cannot independently authorize privileged actions. Completed results emit `agentsec.mcp.result.trust=untrusted_data`. They do not widen `allowed_tools`. MCP-005 (result used as authority) is not this lab.

mcp.question: Can Splunk ALLOW or DENY the tool?
mcp.answer: No. CTRL-MCP-001 runs inside AcmeBank before the handler. Searches read a copy after the fact.

mcp.question: What does Q-MCP-AFTER-DENY returning 0 rows mean?
mcp.answer: No indexed DENY-then-mcp sequence was found for that `run.id`. On a complete copy of RETEST that matches local events, it corroborates the contract. It does not independently prove the runtime never invoked the handler.

mcp.question: Is the DETECT right-hand table OBSERVED runtime evidence?
mcp.answer: No. The DETECT right-hand table is SIMULATED `| makeresults` (`DET-MCP-001-POSITIVE-CONTROL`). It was not indexed. It is not OBSERVED runtime. The hunt fixture `Q-MCP-AFTER-DENY-POSITIVE-CONTROL` is also SIMULATED.

mcp.question: Why is DENY alone not a DET-MCP-001 alert?
mcp.answer: DENY with no later `mcp.started` is the control working (RETEST). The detection asks whether execution began after DENY, not whether a DENY happened.

mcp.question: Why is `mcp.failed` after ALLOW not the same condition as DET-MCP-001?
mcp.answer: `mcp.failed` after ALLOW means the handler began and then errored. There was no DENY. DET-MCP-001 requires DENY then later `mcp.started` for the same run/tool.

mcp.question: Does DET-MCP-001 enforce MCP authorization?
mcp.answer:
No. CTRL-MCP-001 enforces authorization in AcmeBank before the handler. DET-MCP-001 reads a Splunk copy after the fact. Splunk does not ALLOW or DENY the tool.

## Common wrong answers (do not teach these)

- “Zero Splunk rows means the tool was blocked.”
- “ALLOW means the handler ran.”
- “`mcp.started` means success.”
- “`mcp.failed` means prevented.”
- “Unknown tool is DENY.”
- “Known-ungranted tool is ERROR.”
- “The makeresults row is OBSERVED runtime.”
- “Splunk authorized the invoke.”
- “Dashboard Studio proved INV-001.”
